prompts.model:
The Worst Makeover Ever

Last Saturday, I decided to get everything done before my cousin's wedding. It was a big mistake.

In the morning, I had my hair cut at a new salon downtown. The hairdresser talked about her cat the whole time, and when I looked in the mirror, half of my hair was gone! Then I took my suit to the dry cleaner's to get it cleaned. When I picked it up, it was two sizes smaller. Finally, I had my bike repaired, because I wanted to ride to the wedding. Unfortunately, the mechanic forgot to tighten the brakes, and I almost crashed into a mailbox.

In the end, I took a taxi, borrowed my dad's old suit and put on a hat to hide my hair. Everybody laughed, but I laughed too. Next time, I'll do everything myself!

prompts.title: Critique d'une appli
prompts.prompt: Écris la critique d'une application, d'un jeu ou d'un service que tu utilises : par qui il a été créé ou recommandé (passif), ce qu'il offre (relatives : which, that…), et ce que tu changerais si tu pouvais (If I designed…, I would…).

require.label: Utilise la voix passive au moins 3 fois
Au moins 2 pronoms relatifs différents (which, who, that…)
Utilise le conditionnel (would) au moins 2 fois
Organise ton texte en au moins 3 paragraphes

prompts.model:
StudyBuddy: Helpful, but Not Perfect

StudyBuddy is a homework app which our school started using in September. It was created by a small local company, and it was recommended to us by our math teacher.

The app, which is free, lets you take a photo of a problem and explains each step. The explanations are written clearly, and difficult words are translated into French. I also like the timer, which reminds me to take breaks.

However, some answers are given too quickly, so it's tempting to copy them without thinking. If I designed the app, I would hide the final answer until you tried the problem yourself. I would also add a dark mode, because my eyes hurt at night.

Overall, I'd give it four stars. It's a great tool for students who really want to learn.

prompts.title: Plus d'eau chaude !
prompts.prompt: Le chauffe-eau de ton appartement est en panne depuis une semaine. Écris une lettre à ton propriétaire : ce qui s'est passé (break down, run out of…), ce qui n'a pas été fait (passif), et ce que tu feras s'il ne réagit pas.

require.label: Au moins 3 verbes à particule différents (break down, run out of, call back…)
Utilise la voix passive au moins 3 fois
Organise ton texte en au moins 4 paragraphes

prompts.model:
Dear Mr. Petrov,

I am writing about the water heater in apartment six, which broke down last Monday. I called your office the same day, and I was told that a technician would be sent within two days.

Unfortunately, nobody has come to fix it. For a week, my family has had to heat water on the stove to wash. We have also run out of patience, especially since the problem was reported three times. Yesterday, a message was left on your voicemail, but nobody called me back.

If the heater were repaired this week, I would forget the whole story. However, if nothing is done by Friday, I will contact the city's housing services. I would appreciate it if you could get back to me as soon as possible.

Yours sincerely,
Amir Haddad

prompts.title: Le club recrute !
prompts.prompt: Ton club (robotique, théâtre, soccer…) cherche de nouveaux membres. Écris une annonce : ce qu'on fait au club, les gens qui y sont (who, whose), l'endroit où vous vous retrouvez (where), et ce qui se passerait si plus de jeunes s'inscrivaient. Ajoute quelques verbes à particule (sign up, find out…).

require.label: Au moins 4 pronoms relatifs différents (who, which, where, whose…)
Au moins 3 verbes à particule différents (sign up, find out, put off…)
Organise ton texte en au moins 3 paragraphes

prompts.model:
Join the Robotics Club!

Are you someone who loves building things? Do you enjoy solving problems with friends? Then the Robotics Club is the place where you belong!

We meet every Tuesday after school in room twelve, which is next to the science lab. Our coach is Ms. Chen, a computer engineer whose robots have won several competitions. Don't worry if you've never built a robot before. The older members, who started just like you, will help you. You'll learn how to put together motors, sensors and wheels, and how to program them on a laptop.

This year, we are setting up a team for the regional competition in March. If more students signed up, we could build two robots instead of one! So don't put it off: come along next Tuesday and find out what we do. Snacks are provided!

prompts.title: L'affaire du vélo rouge
prompts.prompt: Écris une histoire policière (légère !) : un vélo a disparu devant la bibliothèque. Raconte l'enquête avec les temps du récit (past simple, past continuous, past perfect), des témoins et des indices, puis la solution.

require.label: Utilise le past perfect au moins 4 fois (had locked, had seen…)
Utilise le passé continu au moins 2 fois (was waiting…)
Organise ton texte en au moins 4 paragraphes

prompts.model:
The Case of the Red Bike

It was a rainy Thursday afternoon when Félix came out of the library and stopped dead. His bright red bike, which he had locked to the rack only an hour earlier, had vanished. All that was left was a cut lock lying in a puddle.

Félix looked around. A woman was waiting at the bus stop, and two teenagers were sharing an umbrella across the street. He asked them if they had seen anything. The woman said she had only arrived five minutes before. One of the teenagers, however, remembered that a man in a yellow raincoat had been walking around the bike rack for a long time.

Félix went back inside and spoke to the librarian. She had noticed the same man earlier, because he had asked to borrow a pair of scissors "for a school project". She checked the security camera, and there he was: yellow raincoat, big scissors, red bike.

The next morning, the police found the bike behind a garage on Elm Street. The thief had painted it blue, but he had forgotten one detail: Félix's name was still written under the seat.

prompts.title: Entrevue avec mon grand-père
prompts.prompt: Tu as interviewé un grand-parent (ou un voisin âgé) sur son enfance pour un projet d'école. Écris un article où tu rapportes ses paroles au discours indirect (He told me that…, I asked him whether…, He admitted that…).

require.label: Au moins 5 verbes de discours rapporté différents (said, told, explained, asked, admitted…)
Utilise le past perfect au moins 2 fois (concordance des temps)
Organise ton texte en au moins 4 paragraphes

prompts.model:
Growing Up on a Farm: An Interview with My Grandfather

Last weekend, I interviewed my grandfather, Lucien, about his childhood in Saskatchewan. I wanted to know how different life had been for kids sixty years ago.

First, I asked him what his typical day had looked like. He told me that he used to get up at five every morning to feed the chickens before school. He explained that the school was so small that children of all ages shared the same classroom. When I asked whether he had liked school, he admitted that he had preferred working outside with his father.

Then I asked him about winters. He said they had been much colder than today and that the snow had sometimes covered the fences completely. He remembered that his family had once been stuck at home for a whole week.

Finally, I asked him if he missed those days. He laughed and said that he didn't miss the cold, but that he missed the silence. He told me to put my phone away more often and to listen to the wind. I promised him I would try.

prompts.title: L'uniforme scolaire : pour ou contre ?
prompts.prompt: Le conseil d'élèves propose d'imposer l'uniforme. Rédige un essai argumenté : les arguments pour, les arguments contre, puis ton opinion. Utilise des connecteurs logiques variés (however, although, moreover, therefore, despite…).

require.label: Au moins 4 connecteurs avancés différents (however, although, moreover, despite…)
Utilise au moins 6 mots de liaison différents
Organise ton texte en au moins 4 paragraphes

prompts.model:
Should Students Wear School Uniforms?

In Canada, most public schools do not require uniforms, whereas many private schools do. Recently, our student council suggested introducing them. Although the idea is controversial, it deserves a serious discussion.

Supporters of uniforms argue that they reduce peer pressure. When everyone wears the same clothes, nobody is judged for not having expensive brands. Moreover, parents save time every morning, and they may even save money, since they no longer need to buy so many trendy outfits.

However, many students feel that uniforms limit their freedom of expression. Clothes are a way to show your personality, especially for teenagers. Furthermore, uniforms are not always cheap, and they are often uncomfortable, despite what the companies claim. As a result, some families might actually spend more, not less.

In my opinion, a strict uniform is not the best solution. Nevertheless, a simple dress code, such as a ban on offensive slogans, could solve most of the problems without taking away our individuality. Therefore, I believe our school should choose a dress code rather than a uniform.

prompts.title: Plainte au fournisseur Internet
prompts.prompt: Depuis deux semaines, ton Internet ne fonctionne plus et tu as appelé trois fois le service client. Écris un courriel formel : rapporte ce que chaque agent t'a dit (discours indirect), ce qui s'était passé avant, et ce que tu demandes.

require.label: Au moins 4 verbes de discours rapporté différents (told, said, asked, promised…)
Utilise le past perfect au moins 2 fois
Organise ton texte en au moins 4 paragraphes

prompts.model:
Dear Customer Service Team,

I am writing to complain about the way my internet problem has been handled over the past two weeks.

On March third, my connection stopped working completely. I called your help line, and the first agent told me that there was a problem in my area and that it would be fixed within a day. Two days later, nothing had changed, so I called again. This time, the agent said there was no problem in my area and asked me whether I had restarted my modem. I explained that I had already restarted it several times.

The third agent promised that a technician would come on Saturday morning. I cancelled my plans and waited at home all day, but nobody came. When I called back, I was told that the appointment had never been booked.

As a result, I have been without internet for fourteen days, although I work from home. I would therefore like a full refund for this month and a confirmed appointment with a technician this week. I look forward to your prompt reply.

Sincerely,
Priya Raman

prompts.title: Demande d'informations touristiques
prompts.prompt: Tu prépares un voyage à Vancouver (en famille ou avec ta classe). Écris à l'office de tourisme : présente ton groupe avec des propositions participiales (Having never visited…, Not knowing…) et pose des questions indirectes polies (Could you tell me…? I was wondering whether…).

require.label: Au moins 3 formules de questions indirectes (Could you tell me…, I was wondering…, Do you know…)
Au moins 2 propositions participiales (Having…, Not knowing…, Being…)
Pose au moins 2 questions
Organise ton texte en au moins 4 paragraphes

prompts.model:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am a grade nine teacher from Sherbrooke, Quebec, and I am organizing a five-day trip to Vancouver for my class next May. Having never visited the city myself, I would be very grateful for your advice.

First, could you tell me which neighbourhoods are the safest and most convenient for a large group? We are hoping to stay near public transit, since we will not have a bus. I was also wondering whether any museums offer discounts for school groups.

Secondly, many of my students are passionate about nature. Not knowing the region well, I am not sure which activities are best in spring. Do you know if it is possible to go whale watching at that time of year? And would you happen to know how long it takes to walk to Stanley Park from downtown?

Finally, being on a tight budget, we would like to find some free activities. Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you in advance for your help.

Best regards,
Maude Gagnon

prompts.title: Critique de roman
prompts.prompt: Écris la critique d'un roman (ou d'une série) que tu connais bien : résume le début de l'intrigue sans dévoiler la fin (temps du récit), donne ton avis nuancé avec des connecteurs, et dis à qui tu le recommandes.

require.label: Utilise le past perfect au moins 2 fois
Au moins 2 connecteurs avancés différents (however, although, moreover…)
Organise ton texte en au moins 4 paragraphes

prompts.model:
Anne of Green Gables: Still Charming After a Century

I had always thought that Anne of Green Gables was a book for little kids, so I was surprised by how much I enjoyed it this summer.

The story takes place on Prince Edward Island, where Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert, an elderly brother and sister, have decided to adopt a boy to help on their farm. However, when Matthew arrives at the train station, he finds an eleven-year-old girl with red hair and a lot to say. Someone had made a mistake! Marilla wants to send Anne back, but the girl's imagination and honesty slowly win her over.

What I loved most was Anne's personality. Although she makes one mistake after another, she never gives up, and her dramatic speeches made me laugh out loud. Moreover, the descriptions of the island are so vivid that I now want to visit it. On the other hand, some chapters are a little slow, and the old-fashioned vocabulary can be hard to follow.

Despite these small flaws, I highly recommend this novel to anyone who has ever felt different. It is a perfect book for a rainy weekend, whether you are twelve or fifty.

prompts.title: La fête surprise ratée
prompts.prompt: Raconte la fête surprise que tu as organisée pour un ami… et comment le secret a été découvert. Utilise le past perfect (I had invited…) et le discours indirect (He asked me why…, She told me that…).

require.label: Utilise le past perfect au moins 3 fois
Au moins 3 verbes de discours rapporté différents (told, asked, explained…)
Organise ton texte en au moins 4 paragraphes

prompts.model:
The Surprise That Wasn't

For weeks, I had been planning a surprise party for my best friend Jaden's thirteenth birthday. I had invited everyone from our class, my mom had baked a huge chocolate cake, and we had decorated the basement with balloons. Everything was ready.

On the big day, I told Jaden that we were going to my place to work on our science project. He looked a bit suspicious and asked me why I was wearing my best shirt for a science project. I said that I had spilled juice on all my other shirts. I was quite proud of my answer.

When we arrived, the house was completely dark. Then, just as I opened the door, my little brother Noah ran up to us and shouted, "Jaden! Everybody is hiding in the basement! It's a surprise!" There was a long silence. Somewhere downstairs, someone laughed.

Later, Noah explained that nobody had told him it was a secret. Jaden said it was the best party ever, and he admitted that he had guessed everything the day before anyway, because Maya had asked him what his favourite cake was. So much for secrets!

prompts.title: Rapport sur le sondage du quartier
prompts.prompt: Ton comité de quartier a fait un sondage sur la circulation et les parcs. Rédige un rapport pour la ville : introduction, résultats, recommandations, conclusion. Utilise des connecteurs et des collocations (make a decision, take action, pay attention…).

require.label: Au moins 3 verbes de collocation différents (make a decision, take action, pay attention…)
Utilise au moins 6 mots de liaison différents
Organise ton texte en au moins 4 paragraphes

prompts.model:
Report on the Maplewood Neighbourhood Survey

Introduction
The aim of this report is to summarize the results of our survey on traffic and green spaces, and to make recommendations to the city council. More than one hundred residents took part in the survey in October.

Main findings
Most residents said that they felt unsafe crossing Park Avenue, especially in the morning. Several parents complained that drivers did not pay attention to the school zone. Moreover, many people mentioned that the small park on Birch Street had been neglected for years: the benches are broken and the playground is old. On the other hand, residents were very positive about the community garden. Although it was only created last spring, it has already become a popular meeting place.

Recommendations
First, the city should take action quickly by adding a pedestrian crossing near the school. Second, we suggest renovating the Birch Street park, since this would make a real difference for young families. Finally, the council should consider creating a second community garden.

Conclusion
In short, residents care deeply about safety and green spaces. We hope the council will make a decision before next spring.

prompts.title: Le jour où j'ai raté l'autobus
prompts.prompt: Raconte un moment où un petit détail a tout changé dans ta vie (vrai ou inventé). Imagine ce qui se serait passé si les choses avaient été différentes (If I hadn't…, I would have…) et exprime un regret ou un soulagement (If only…, I wish I had…).

require.label: Utilise le conditionnel passé (would have…) au moins 4 fois
Utilise if, if only et I wish
Utilise le past perfect au moins 3 fois (If I had…)
Organise ton texte en au moins 4 paragraphes

prompts.model:
The Day I Missed the Bus

Three years ago, on a cold Tuesday in February, I missed the school bus by about ten seconds. At the time, it felt like a disaster. Looking back, it was one of the luckiest moments of my life.

Since I had no other choice, I decided to walk to school through the park. Halfway there, I heard someone calling for help. An elderly man had slipped on the ice and couldn't get up. I called nine-one-one and stayed with him until the paramedics arrived. If I had caught the bus, nobody would have found him for a long time, because the park was empty that morning.

A week later, the man, Mr. Okafor, came to my school to thank me. He turned out to be a retired science teacher, and he offered to help me prepare for the science fair. If he hadn't coached me, I would never have won first prize, and I probably wouldn't be dreaming of becoming an engineer today.

I used to wish I hadn't been so slow that morning. Now I think the opposite. If only I had known then what a difference those ten seconds would make!

prompts.title: Mystère dans la cuisine
prompts.prompt: Ce matin, ta cuisine est sens dessus dessous : fenêtre ouverte, pain disparu, traces de pattes… Écris un article pour le journal de l'école où tu fais des hypothèses sur ce qui a dû se passer (must have, can't have, might have) avant de résoudre le mystère.

require.label: Au moins 3 modaux différents pour tes hypothèses (must have, can't have, might have…)
Fais au moins 5 hypothèses avec un modal
Organise ton texte en au moins 4 paragraphes

prompts.model:
Mystery in the Kitchen

When I came downstairs this morning, our kitchen looked as if a tornado had passed through it. The window was wide open, a loaf of bread had disappeared, and there were muddy footprints all over the counter.

My first suspect was my brother Liam, who is always hungry. However, he can't have done it, because he was at a sleepover last night. My parents can't have done it either: they went to bed early, and besides, they never climb on the counter.

The footprints were small, with five long toes, almost like tiny hands. It might have been a squirrel, but squirrels don't usually like bread that much. Then I noticed that the garbage can had been knocked over and that the lid of the compost bin was missing. Only one animal in our neighbourhood is clever enough to do that. It must have been a raccoon!

My mom thinks I should have closed the window before going to bed. She's probably right. The raccoon must have smelled the bread from the backyard and decided to have a midnight snack. Tonight, I'll keep the window shut and set up my phone to film the kitchen. Case closed… I hope.

prompts.title: Une semaine de fou au bureau
prompts.prompt: Ta collègue est en vacances. Écris-lui un courriel pour raconter la semaine catastrophique (mais qui finit bien) que tu viens de vivre au travail. Utilise au moins 4 expressions idiomatiques de façon naturelle (a piece of cake, under the weather, the last straw, call it a day…).

require.label: Au moins 4 expressions idiomatiques différentes (under the weather, the last straw, a piece of cake…)
Utilise le passé simple anglais (au moins 6 verbes)
Organise ton texte en au moins 4 paragraphes

prompts.model:
Hi Jasmine,

I hope your vacation in Nova Scotia is going well, because things here have been crazy. Let me tell you about my week.

On Monday, our boss announced that the Bergeron project had to be finished by Friday instead of next month. He said it would be a piece of cake. It wasn't. To make things worse, half the team was under the weather, so Daniel and I had to hit the books and learn the new software in two days.

On Wednesday, the client called. Instead of beating around the bush, she told us directly that she hated the design. That was almost the last straw. Daniel wanted to cut corners and just change the colours, but I refused. We stayed until midnight and redesigned everything from scratch.

On Friday, we presented the new version. To our surprise, the client loved it and asked us to work on two more projects. In the end, her criticism was a blessing in disguise. At six o'clock, we finally called it a day and went out for pizza.

Now the ball is in your court: when you come back, you're in charge of the next project! I'm going to hit the sack early tonight.

Cheers,
Omar

prompts.title: Jeux vidéo : perte de temps ou outil ?
prompts.prompt: Rédige un essai : les jeux vidéo sont-ils une perte de temps ou un outil utile ? Présente les deux côtés et conclus. Enrichis ton vocabulaire avec des mots construits (préfixes et suffixes : unhealthy, creativity, harmless, enjoyable…).

require.label: Au moins 4 mots construits avec un préfixe ou un suffixe (unhealthy, creativity, harmless…)
Utilise au moins 6 mots de liaison différents
Organise ton texte en au moins 4 paragraphes

prompts.model:
Video Games: A Waste of Time or a Useful Tool?

Video games are one of the most popular forms of entertainment in the world, yet many parents still see them as a complete waste of time. In my view, the reality is more complicated.

To begin with, many games encourage creativity and problem-solving. Building games allow players to design entire cities, while strategy games require careful planning and patience. Moreover, online games can strengthen friendships, since teenagers often play and chat with classmates. Some teachers even use educational games because they make learning more enjoyable and effective.

Nevertheless, games are not completely harmless. Overuse can lead to an unhealthy lifestyle: players who spend hours in front of a screen move less and often sleep badly. Some games are also designed to be addictive, with rewards that keep players coming back. As a result, homework and family relationships may suffer.

In conclusion, video games are neither good nor bad in themselves. What matters is how they are used. With reasonable limits and responsible choices, they can be a source of fun and even improvement. Without such limits, however, they can easily become a problem.

prompts.title: Lettre d'excuses
prompts.prompt: Tu as complètement oublié le dîner de départ à la retraite de ta mentore au travail. Écris-lui une lettre d'excuses : ce qui s'est passé, ce que tu aurais dû faire (should have / shouldn't have), ce qui serait différent si… (conditionnels mixtes), et comment tu vas te rattraper.

require.label: Utilise should have ET shouldn't have
Utilise le conditionnel (would have, wouldn't be…) au moins 3 fois
Utilise au moins une phrase avec if + past perfect
Organise ton texte en au moins 4 paragraphes

prompts.model:
Dear Hélène,

I owe you a huge apology. Last Friday, I completely missed your farewell lunch, and I have felt terrible about it all weekend.

I have no excuse, but here is what happened. That morning, a client called with an urgent problem, and I spent three hours on the phone. By the time I looked at the clock, it was half past two and everyone had already left the restaurant. I should have written the lunch in my calendar, and I definitely shouldn't have answered that call without checking the time. If I had been more organized, I would have been there to give my speech and to thank you for everything.

You have been my mentor since my very first day at the company. If you hadn't trained me so patiently, I wouldn't be doing this job today. That is why missing your lunch hurts so much.

I would love to make it up to you. Could I take you out for dinner next week, at the restaurant of your choice? This time, I promise to switch off my phone.

With my sincere apologies and gratitude,
Marc

prompts.title: Message à l'équipe après la finale
prompts.prompt: Ton équipe (hockey, soccer, robotique…) a perdu la finale de justesse. Écris un message à ton équipe : ce qui aurait pu se passer autrement (If we had…, we would have…), ce que vous auriez dû faire (should have, could have), et pourquoi tu es quand même fier/fière.

require.label: Utilise le conditionnel passé (would have…) au moins 3 fois

prompts.model:

See you at practice,
Zoé

prompts.title: Pourquoi faire du bénévolat ?

prompts.model:
Why Volunteering Matters

When I retired last year, a few friends warned me that I would get bored. They were wrong. Thanks to volunteering, I have hardly had a free afternoon since.

Every Tuesday, I help at the local food bank. Few people realize how many families in our town depend on it. Some of them have little money left after paying rent, and many are working parents, not only the unemployed. On Thursdays, I visit the elderly at a care home near my house. Neither of the two residents I see regularly has family nearby, so a little conversation means a lot to them.

Volunteering is not only about helping others, however. It has changed my whole life. I have met people from all backgrounds, learned to cook for a hundred people and discovered talents I never knew I had. Most importantly, I feel useful.

If you have even a little free time, I encourage you to try it. You don't need any special skills: a smile and a pair of hands will do. None of us can solve every problem alone, but together we can make a real difference.

prompts.title: Ce que j'aurais aimé savoir
prompts.prompt: Un(e) ami(e) commence l'école secondaire (ou un nouvel emploi) la semaine prochaine. Écris-lui un courriel : ce que tu aurais aimé savoir à tes débuts (I wish I had known…), les erreurs que tu aurais pu éviter (If I had…, I would have…), et tes conseils.

require.label: Utilise I wish ET If only + past perfect

prompts.model:
Hi Ethan,

I can't believe you're starting high school next week! Two years ago, I was in your shoes, and I made quite a few mistakes. So here's the advice I wish someone had given me.

First, get organized from day one. I wish I had used an agenda in grade nine. I forgot two major assignments in the first month, and if I had written them down, I wouldn't have lost so many marks. Trust me, it's not rocket science, but it makes a huge difference.

Second, don't be shy. During my first weeks, I ate lunch alone because I was too nervous to talk to anyone. If only I had joined a club sooner! When I finally signed up for the improv team in November, I made friends right away. If I hadn't been so scared, I would have enjoyed those first months much more.

Finally, ask for help. I would have saved myself a lot of stress if I had talked to my teachers earlier. They might seem strict, but most of them are really kind if you talk to them after class. You should never be afraid to say you don't understand.

Good luck, and remember: everyone feels lost at first!

Cheers,
Maya

prompts.title: Réclamation à l'hôtel
prompts.prompt: Tu as séjourné dans un hôtel qui ne ressemblait pas du tout à sa publicité. prompts.model:

When I informed the reception staff, I was assured that a technician would assist us the following morning. No technician ever came. Never have I been treated with such indifference by a hotel.

Furthermore, the so-called private beach was closed for the entire week, a fact that nobody mentioned when we made our reservation. What disappointed my children most was that the swimming pool, the main reason we had chosen your resort, was also out of service.

I fully understand that unexpected problems do occur. However, I would have expected to be informed in advance and offered an alternative. Under the circumstances, I believe that a partial refund is entirely justified. I would therefore be grateful if you could reimburse half of the total amount, namely six hundred dollars.

I look forward to receiving your reply within two weeks. Should I not hear from you by then, I will have no choice but to share my experience on travel review websites.

prompts.model:
Talk Like a Canadian: A Survival Guide for New Students

Welcome to our school! Whether you have just arrived from Paris, Mumbai or Mexico City, you have probably noticed that Canadians speak English in their own special way. Don't panic. Here is everything you need to survive your first winter, linguistically speaking.

Let's start with the basics. If you need the toilet, ask for the washroom: here, that word is far more common than "restroom" or "loo". When the temperature drops below zero, you will need a toque, which is a warm knitted hat. And if a teacher calls you a keener, take it as a compliment… mostly. It means you are extremely enthusiastic about school.

Money can be confusing, too. A one-dollar coin is called a loonie, because there is a loon on it, and a two-dollar coin is a toonie. If your friend offers to buy you a pop, they mean a soft drink. And if someone in a coffee shop orders a double-double, they want a coffee with two creams and two sugars.

Finally, there is the famous little word "eh". Canadians sometimes add it at the end of a sentence to ask for agreement: "Nice day, eh?" Use it with care, though. Overdo it and you will sound like a tourist!

What you really need to know, however, is that Canadians are generally patient with newcomers. So don't be afraid to ask questions, eh?

prompts.model:
Is Remote Work the Future of Work?

Since the pandemic, remote work has moved from the margins to the mainstream. It is widely believed that this change is permanent; however, the reality appears to be more nuanced.

The advantages of working from home are considerable. The elimination of daily commuting is arguably the most obvious benefit, both for employees, who gain time and money, and for the environment. Moreover, many workers report an improvement in concentration once they are freed from the interruptions of an open-plan office. Parents, in particular, tend to appreciate the flexibility it offers.

Nevertheless, remote work is not without its drawbacks. The absence of face-to-face contact seems to weaken team spirit, and young employees are likely to suffer most, since they learn a great deal by observing experienced colleagues. Furthermore, the boundary between professional and private life tends to disappear when the kitchen table becomes an office. For some, this leads to longer hours rather than greater freedom.

It is therefore unlikely that the traditional office will vanish altogether. A more probable outcome is the generalization of hybrid models, in which employees divide their time between home and the workplace. Such arrangements may combine the autonomy of remote work with the social benefits of the office.

In conclusion, remote work is here to stay, but probably not in its most extreme form. The real challenge for employers will be the creation of a balance that serves both productivity and well-being.

Background

An informal survey conducted at our spring fair showed strong interest in such a service.

Tools would be lent for up to one week, and members would be asked to pay a modest annual fee of twenty dollars. The service could be run by volunteers on Saturday mornings and Wednesday evenings.

At noon, I rushed to the library. After all, where else do stories sleep? The room was almost empty. Then I noticed that someone had left a book on the librarian's desk, open at a page about famous explorers. In the margin, someone had drawn a tiny arrow pointing at the window. No sooner had I looked outside than I saw it: a huge banner hanging from the gym roof that read "HAPPY BIRTHDAY, AMIR!"

It was my best friend Chloé who had organized the whole treasure hunt. She had been planning it for weeks with half the class, who were now hiding behind the bookshelves, trying not to laugh. Only then did I remember that it was actually my birthday. I had been so busy studying for exams that I had completely forgotten.

Never have I been so happy to be fooled.

prompts.model:
Should Cars Be Banned from City Centres?

Few urban debates are as heated as the one surrounding the private car. For some, it embodies freedom; for others, it poses a threat to public health and quality of life. Although an outright ban is appealing in theory, I would argue that a gradual approach is both fairer and more effective.

The case against cars in city centres is compelling. Traffic congestion wastes time, emissions degrade air quality, and streets designed for vehicles leave little room for pedestrians, cyclists or children at play. Cities that have pedestrianized their historic cores often report livelier streets and thriving local businesses, albeit after an initial period of resistance from merchants.

Nonetheless, it must be borne in mind that not everyone can simply switch to cycling or public transit. Elderly residents, people with disabilities and tradespeople who carry heavy equipment depend on vehicles, and a sudden ban would hit them hardest. Moreover, in many Canadian cities, public transit is neither frequent nor extensive enough to absorb a sudden surge in demand, particularly in winter.

A sensible compromise would therefore be to strike a balance: restrict access progressively, provided that reliable alternatives are put in place first. Expanding bus networks, creating protected bike lanes and offering exemptions for those who genuinely need a car would make the transition far more acceptable.

It is high time cities stopped treating the car as untouchable. Yet if we are to draw any conclusion from past reforms, it is that change imposed too quickly tends to provoke a backlash. Hence the need for ambition tempered by pragmatism.

prompts.model:
Choose Your Words Carefully

Imagine two people describing the same classmate. One says she is determined; the other calls her stubborn. Neither is lying, yet the first sounds like a compliment and the second like a complaint. Welcome to the fascinating world of connotation.

Many English words share a basic meaning but carry very different emotional baggage. Slim and skinny both describe someone who is not heavy, but whereas slim sounds elegant, skinny often suggests that something is wrong. Similarly, a curious neighbour is pleasantly interested in the world; a nosy one is interfering in your business. The same goes for money: if you are thrifty, you manage your budget wisely, but if you are stingy, you refuse to share even when you could easily afford to.

Sometimes the difference is subtle enough to cause real misunderstandings. Telling a friend that her new jacket looks inexpensive is a tactful observation; telling her it looks cheap may end the friendship. Calling an adult childlike praises their sense of wonder, whereas calling them childish criticizes their immaturity. And while a famous scientist is admired, a notorious one is known for all the wrong reasons.

For French speakers, this is a particular trap, as bilingual dictionaries rarely mention these shades of meaning. The best strategy is to read widely and notice how native speakers use each word. After all, the right word does not merely describe a person; it reveals what you think of them. So the next time you are tempted to call someone arrogant, ask yourself whether confident might be fairer.

prompts.model:
The Science Fair Disaster

All year, Karim had been looking forward to the regional science fair. He and his best friend Sofia had come up with what they believed was a brilliant idea: a solar-powered lunch box that kept food warm without electricity. For weeks, they put up with burnt fingers, melted plastic and Karim's little brother, who kept asking whether he could eat the experiments.

The night before the fair, everything seemed perfect. Karim was so confident that he told everyone they were going to win. His grandmother simply smiled and said, "Don't count your chickens before they hatch."

The next morning, it turned out she was right. The sky was grey, rain was pouring down, and the gym where the fair took place had no windows. Without sunlight, their lunch box was just an ordinary box. When the judges came across their table, the soup inside was stone cold. Karim wanted to run away and hide.

Instead, Sofia came up with a plan. She grabbed a desk lamp, plugged it in and calmly explained how the system would work on a sunny day. The judges were impressed by her quick thinking, and the team ended up with an honourable mention.

It took Karim a few days to get over his disappointment, but he learned his lesson. The following year, he didn't brag about anything until the results were announced. As his grandmother likes to say, don't count your chickens before they hatch.

prompts.model:
Artificial Intelligence in the Classroom: Friend or Foe?

When chatbots capable of writing essays in seconds became widely available, many teachers reacted with alarm. Some schools banned them outright; others chose to embrace them. Both reactions are understandable, but neither, in my view, addresses the real question: what is school actually for?

If the purpose of education is merely to produce correct answers, then AI undoubtedly poses a serious threat. A student who outsources every assignment learns nothing, and teachers can no longer be certain whose work they are marking. Bear in mind, too, that these tools sometimes produce confident but entirely false information, which inexperienced users are unlikely to detect.

Conversely, if school exists to teach young people how to think, AI could arguably become a valuable ally. Used wisely, it can explain a concept in several different ways, generate practice questions or give instant feedback on a first draft. Students who would never dare to ask a question in class might well do so in front of a screen, albeit only if they remain the authors of their own ideas.

The challenge, then, is to strike a balance. Rather than pretending the technology does not exist, schools should teach students to use it critically: to check sources, to question answers and to acknowledge their use of it. Assessment will also have to evolve, with more oral presentations and in-class writing.

Will teachers manage to adapt quickly enough? I suspect so, provided that they are given the time and training they need. One conclusion can already be drawn: banning AI is no longer an option; teaching with it is.

It is not every day that a circus show makes an entire audience gasp, giggle and hold its breath within the space of five minutes. Yet that is exactly what the young troupe behind Gravity, Optional achieved at our community theatre last Saturday, albeit not without a few wobbles.

The opening number is simply breathtaking. Six acrobats stride onto a bare stage and, within seconds, climb on top of one another as though gravity were merely a suggestion. A juggler then stumbles across the stage, apparently on the verge of collapse, before catching seven clubs behind his back without even glancing at them. The children in the front row were giggling uncontrollably, while their parents chuckled at the clever wordplay hidden in the narration.

However, the second half is noticeably weaker. A long aerial routine, though technically flawless, drags on for far too long, and the recorded music is so loud that the narrator's whispered jokes are lost entirely. At one point, a toddler behind me muttered, "Is it finished?", which rather summed up the mood. Fortunately, the finale recaptures the magic: the entire cast floats above the audience on silk ribbons, as if the theatre ceiling had suddenly vanished.

Overall, Gravity, Optional is an ambitious, joyful and occasionally self-indulgent show. Trim twenty minutes and it would be close to perfect. Even so, families looking for an unforgettable evening should not hesitate. Just be prepared to stare upward with your mouth wide open, as if you were five years old again.

prompts.title: Le bilinguisme officiel : atout ou fardeau ?

prompts.model:
Is Official Bilingualism Worth the Effort?

Since the Official Languages Act was passed in nineteen sixty-nine, Canada has defined itself as a country with two official languages. More than half a century later, the policy still provokes debate. Some regard it as a cornerstone of national identity; others dismiss it as a costly symbol with little relevance to their daily lives. Both views, I would argue, miss part of the picture.

The benefits of bilingualism are difficult to overstate. On a practical level, it guarantees that French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians can deal with their federal government in their own language, which is hardly a trivial matter in a democracy. Bilingual individuals, moreover, enjoy wider career prospects, particularly in the public service, tourism and international trade. There is also a cultural dimension: a second language opens the door to literature, music and humour that would otherwise remain inaccessible.

Nonetheless, critics raise legitimate concerns. In many regions, French is rarely heard, and immersion programs are not always available, let alone well funded. Bilingual services undeniably come at a cost, and some argue that this money would be better spent elsewhere. Others point out that Indigenous languages, which predate both English and French, receive comparatively little recognition.

These objections deserve to be taken seriously, but they are arguments for improving the policy rather than abandoning it. Bilingualism need not come at the expense of other languages; on the contrary, a society that values two languages is arguably better placed to value many.

Ultimately, bilingualism is less a burden than an investment, albeit one whose returns are not always immediately visible. As any learner knows, the effort is considerable. So, in the end, are the rewards.

prompts.model:
Why English Spelling Is Out to Get You

Every French speaker learning English eventually reaches the same moment of despair. You have mastered the grammar, you have memorized hundreds of phrasal verbs, and then someone asks you to read the word "Wednesday" aloud. Is the first d silent? I'm afraid so. And the second e? That one too.

Silent letters are the first trap. The k in knife and knight has been quiet for centuries, the b in doubt and comb never says a word, and the s in island seems to have been added purely to annoy learners. Even the h at the start of hour and honest stays silent, whereas in hotel and happy it is perfectly audible. Is there a logical rule? Not really.

Then come the homophones. Weather and whether sound identical, as do flour and flower, which explains why my first attempt at writing a cake recipe in English involved a bouquet. Fortunately, context usually saves the day, or so I hope.

But the true villain is the combination -ough. Though, through, tough, thought and cough each rhyme with something different. Native speakers rarely notice, of course; they learned these words long before they could question them.

So what is a learner to do? Listen carefully, read aloud as often as possible and accept that some mistakes are inevitable. As the proverb goes, practice makes perfect, or at least slightly less embarrassing. Will you ever pronounce receipt correctly on the first try? Perhaps not. But every cloud has a silver lining: with English, you will never be bored.
